name: Room Additions vs. ADUs and Garage Conversions in Los Angeles
headline: Room Additions vs. ADUs and Garage Conversions in Los Angeles
articleBody: Although room additions, accessory dwelling units (ADUs), and garage conversions can all add space, California law and Los Angeles regulations treat them differently. A **room addition** typically expands the existing primary dwelling’s habitable area without creating a separate dwelling unit. Zoning and building departments treat it as part of the main residence, applying standard setbacks, floor area ratio, and parking rules for the lot. By contrast, state ADU laws—summarized by the California Department of Housing and Community Development—establish **statewide mandates** that cities and counties must allow ADUs and junior ADUs under specific criteria, often with relaxed parking and density restrictions. Los Angeles’ local ADU ordinances implement these state requirements, setting size limits (such as maximum square footage relative to the primary home), height, and placement rules that can be more flexible than those for a simple addition. Garage conversions can be either **converted ADUs** or simply new living space attached to the main home. Building code guidance stresses that converting a garage to habitable space requires upgrades like insulation, raised floor, egress, and sometimes structural modifications. When the conversion is an ADU, additional requirements for separate kitchen, bathroom, and sometimes independent utility metering may apply. Local planning and building department FAQs note that ADUs often benefit from streamlined approvals due to state law, while a large room addition may be constrained more by local mansionization or FAR limits. However, ADUs must meet separate unit standards, which can increase cost and complexity relative to a non-independent room addition. Homeowners evaluating options are often advised by planners and housing agencies to consider long-term use: ADUs can generate rental income or house extended family more independently, while room additions integrate into the existing home’s circulation and are governed by the primary dwelling’s zoning limits.
